A.explanation: Both columns are swapped. A $\gamma$-ray is not an electron and a $\beta^-$ particle is not electromagnetic radiation.

B.explanation: The $\gamma$-ray part is correct, but a helium-4 nucleus describes an $\alpha$-particle, not a $\beta^-$ particle.

C.explanation: A $\gamma$-ray is high-frequency electromagnetic radiation and a $\beta^-$ particle is a high-speed electron emitted from the nucleus.

D.explanation: Both are wrong. A high-speed electron is $\beta^-$ not $\gamma$, and a helium-4 nucleus is $\alpha$ not $\beta^-$.

hints: Look at the three phrases in the table: electromagnetic radiation, high-speed electron and helium-4 nucleus - one belongs to alpha, one to beta-minus and one to gamma.
Recall that $\gamma$ has no charge and no rest mass, travels at the speed of light and is not deflected by electric or magnetic fields.
Recall that $\beta^-$ is emitted when a neutron in the nucleus changes to a proton, ejecting a fast-moving electron, while a helium-4 nucleus is the $\alpha$-particle.
walkthrough: Identify what the table asks: match $\gamma$-ray in the first column and $\beta^-$ particle in the second column to the correct physical nature.
State the rule for $\gamma$: it is part of the electromagnetic spectrum, a photon of very high frequency with zero charge and (effectively) zero rest mass.
State the rule for $\beta^-$: it is an electron, charge $-e$, created and ejected at high speed during $\beta^-$ decay when a neutron becomes a proton.
Recall for elimination that an $\alpha$-particle is a helium-4 nucleus, with charge $+2e$ and mass of about $4u$, so any row using helium-4 nucleus for $\beta^-$ is wrong.
Compare with the rows: only electromagnetic radiation for $\gamma$-ray paired with high-speed electron for $\beta^-$ particle satisfies both rules. This is option C.
